Description
📄 Want your resume roasted in a future video? Submit it here: https://forms.gle/V5XniewCDENxMhrn8
⚡ Get direct AI Engineer career coaching: https://aiengineer.community/join

I roasted two real resumes from engineers in my program who are trying to pivot their software careers into AI engineering: a software architect with 10+ years of experience and a cloud support engineer two years in. Neither resume mentions AI once, and both are missing the same thing: a clear story that leads into an AI engineering role. As an ex-GitHub engineer who reviews resumes like these every week, I walk through what I would change on each page, from cutting to a single page to building the one AI project that bridges your existing experience into the job you want.

What You'll Learn

- Why a two-page resume works against you even with 10+ years of experience (and what to cut first)
- The "no clear story" problem that keeps software architects and cloud engineers out of AI roles
- How a North Star AI project bridges your current experience into AI engineering
- Why explicit numbers ("a thousand releases with zero downtime") beat lines recruiters have to take on faith
- Where to put personal projects so they get read, instead of buried under Additional Information
- How to reframe data infrastructure experience as the foundation for AI pipelines
- Why I keep resumes in LaTeX or Markdown and let Claude Code fact-check every application
- The certification trick: embed certs inside your work experience bullets with proof links
- Why artifacts like GitHub links convince recruiters faster than corporate jargon

Timestamps
0:00 Two resumes trying to pivot into AI engineering
0:18 Resume 1: the 10-year software architect
1:41 Work experience: ownership and explicit numbers
3:56 No clear story into AI engineering
4:35 Fix: build a North Star AI project
5:25 Structural fixes to get to one page
8:49 Resume 2: the cloud support engineer
10:03 Projects buried under Additional Information
11:35 The leftover "seeking SRE role" line
11:46 Let Claude Code fact-check your resume
12:24 Reframe infrastructure skills for AI pipelines
14:21 Certifications: keep, cut, or embed them
15:47 What both resumes did right
16:28 Too much jargon, not enough artifacts
17:21 Land your AI engineering job

Why I Made This Video
Most engineers in my program can already do the AI engineering work they are applying for, and still get filtered out on the resume. I wanted to show, on two real resumes, what I would change before sending a single application.

Zen critiques two resumes for pivoting into AI engineering. Key topics: keeping resume to one page,...
Zen critiques two resumes for pivoting into AI engineering. Key topics: keeping resume to one page, creating a clear narrative/bridge from current experience to AI, building a 'North Star' AI project (e.g., scalable data pipeline), replacing fluffy summaries with concrete achievements, showing skills through projects rather than listing them, limiting old roles to 3 bullet points, eliminating redundant skills sections, inserting certifications into work experience context, and adding hyperlinks to GitHub/project artifacts. He stresses reframing existing DevOps/cloud experience around AI systems and avoiding corporate jargon. Major claim: a strong capstone project that leverages existing skills is more critical than nitpicking each bullet point.

Description
This session offers a detailed look at the architectures involved in Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) and Large Language Model Operations (LLMOps). It's designed for those interested in the technical specifics and practical applications of MLOps and LLMOps, including the key components and workflows that define these fields.   Attendees will learn about: The core architectures used in MLOps and LLMOps. The various elements involved in these operations, such as data management, model training, deployment, and monitoring. Strategies for implementing effective MLOps and LLMOps in your projects, with a focus on improving efficiency and model performance.
 
Talk By: Arpit Jasapara, Software Engineer, Databricks  ; Joseph Bradley, Principal Product Specialist, Databricks  ; Yinxi Zhang, Staff Data Scientist, Databricks  
 
Here's more to explore:
LLM Compact Guide: https://dbricks.co/43WuQyb
Big Book of MLOps: https://dbricks.co/3r0Pqiz
 
Connect with us: Website: https://databricks.com
Twitter: https://twitter.com/databricks 
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/data…
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/databricksinc
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/databricksinc
Databricks MLOps and LMOps architecture best practices. MLOps combines data ops, DevOps, and model ...
Databricks MLOps and LMOps architecture best practices. MLOps combines data ops, DevOps, and model ops; key practices include role separation (business stakeholder, data engineer, data scientist, ML engineer, data governance officer), environment isolation across dev/staging/prod, promoting code (not just models) for reproducibility and production data lockdown, Unity Catalog for centralized governance/lineage of tables, features, models, and inference tables, plus model serving (real-time APIs, A/B testing, canary deployments, request/response logging) and monitoring for drift. Databricks MLOps Stacks provide a customizable CI/CD framework integrating GitHub/Azure DevOps. For LMOps: RAG architectures using vector search, feature serving, foundation model APIs, CPU model serving for chains, MLflow tracing and evaluation (LLM-as-a-judge metrics, answer relevance, human feedback logging), config-based LangChain chains, auto-synced vector indexes, and inference/feedback tables for monitoring and fine-tuning. Pre-training/fine-tuning stacks include Mosaic AI model training, Composer, streaming datasets, LLM Foundry, evaluation gauntlet, and DBRX, with Spark/Delta/Unity Catalog remaining core. AI security guidance referenced via Databricks whitepaper.

Josh (7 yrs at Google, DoorDash, ZS) explains data engineer resume optimization. 80% of resumes auto-rejected by ATS; recruiters spend 6-8 seconds, hiring managers 30-60 sec. Must-have sections: header (no photo/tagline), skills grouped logically, experience, projects (critical for entry-level), education + third-party certs (AWS, Databricks). Bullet formula: action verb + specific tech + measurable impact (e.g., 'built Spark-based ETL processing 2TB daily, reducing latency 60%'; 'migrated 40+ Airflow DAGs cutting cost $180k/yr'; 'Snowflake data model serving 200+ analysts'). Common mistakes: no quantifiable impact, tech stack mismatch with JD, wrong length (1-1.5 pages for mid-level, 2 for 8+ yrs), fancy formatting (tables/graphics break ATS), vague projects. Entry-level: projects 30-40% of space, education top; experienced: experience is main focus, old roles summarized. Tools: open-source Resume Matcher (local Docker setup) and VMock (free ATS scoring). No need for 50 resumes; start with master, create 3-4 flavors per role. Sponsor: Data Vidya (DE-specific prep platform).

The transcript demonstrates a complete Mac development environment setup for agentic engineering, e...
The transcript demonstrates a complete Mac development environment setup for agentic engineering, emphasizing reproducibility via Nix, Nix Darwin (macOS settings), Home Manager (user-level config), and dotfiles. Key tools installed include Wezterm, Neovim with plugins (Lazy, snacks, oil, neoit, git signs, which-key), Starship shell prompt, and the Herd terminal multiplexer (preferred over tmux). The user configures Claude Code and creates a global agent memory file (agents.md) with rules to enforce quality, avoid mdash, and prioritize long-term maintainability. The entire setup is reproducible via a single rebuild script.

Description
In this video, I’ll show you how to write a winning tech resume that stands out to hiring managers, even in today’s competitive tech job market. With over 22 years of experience as a software engineer, tech interviewer, and career coach, I’ve reviewed hundreds of resumes. I’ll walk you through my process for rewriting a resume from scratch—using my personal experience landing a job at Google.

I’ll cover:
● Common tech resume mistakes and how to fix them
● How to highlight your technical and soft skills
● Writing a professional summary that makes an impact
● How to optimize your LinkedIn profile to complement your resume
● The best AI tools for resume optimization
● Practical resume tips for landing your next tech job
● If you’re struggling to land roles, this video is for you!

🔑 Key Topics:
● Tech resume tips
● Resume optimization
● Job market strategies
● Resume rewrite examples
● Software engineering job search

A 22-year software engineer and career coach explains how to write a winning tech resume for 2025. ...
A 22-year software engineer and career coach explains how to write a winning tech resume for 2025. Key points: common resume flaws (lack of impact, context, presuming reader knowledge), six required sections (name/contact, professional summary, skills, experience, projects, education), the Resume Formula (Accomplished X as measured by Y by doing Z), finding impact metrics from external/internal sources, reading job descriptions to extract keywords (technical skills, soft skills, product qualities), reflecting on experience, using tools like ChatGPT and SkillSyncer to optimize. Emphasizes tailoring to job descriptions and minimizing whitespace.

Description
The budget has landed. Investors are reacting. But do the old rules of property investing still apply, or is Australia entering a new era of wealth creation through real estate?

In this episode of The Smart Property Investment Show, host Liam Garman sits down with Australian Property Scouts’ Sam Gordon to unpack whether we’re witnessing a reset of Australia’s property market in real time, and what investors need to do to stay ahead of it.

Gordon breaks down which suburbs and regions are best positioned to thrive in the years ahead, and which areas risk being left behind as the market evolves.

He also discusses the findings of the newly released APS Whitepaper, challenging the federal government’s prediction that rents will rise by just $2 a week. Gordon argues the impact could be far more significant, with rental increases of up to 40 per cent in some markets. You can view the whitepaper here.

Despite the doom and gloom dominating headlines, Gordon says the latest tax changes are unlikely to derail sophisticated investors, estimating they will pay around 6.5 per cent more in tax under the new settings.

So, are we witnessing the end of the old property playbook, or simply the start of a smarter one?

Hi my name is Chris and I build productivity apps (Mogul, Ellie, Luna and Lily) 👋

In this video I talk about more "advanced" iOS design tips that I use in my owns app to make them feel 10x better (in my opinion) than the default iOS apps. This is from personal experience but also studying the top iOS apps out there and I hope it helps :)

✨ CHECK OUT MOBBIN (& 20% off your first year)  ✨
https://mobbin.com/raroque

----

My apps and socials: https://chrisraroque.com
My agency (work with me): https://aloa.co/

Timestamps:
0:00 - Intro / What we are covering today
0:32 - Interactions & Animations (tip 1)
2:47 - Custom illustrations (tip 2)
4:52 - Haptic feedback (tip 3)
6:06 - Good icons (tip 4)
8:56 - Elevate your design taste (tip 5)
10:53 - Final thoughts and thanks for watching :)

#appdevelopment #dayinthelife #softwareengineer #startup #softwaredev #indieappdeveloper #dayinthelifecoding #codewithme #buildinpublic #vlog
iOS app design techniques to make apps feel more polished than default Apple apps. Specific advance...
iOS app design techniques to make apps feel more polished than default Apple apps. Specific advanced tips: add custom animations (e.g., sliding page transitions in tab switches, multi-step animation sequences like rotating send button into check mark, expanding background, spring text fades); use AI coding tools like Claude Code to implement animations by breaking interactions into sub-steps rather than oneshotting. Use custom illustrations for empty states, generated by AI or commissioned artists, with variations (e.g., Lily the ghost mascot in meeting app Lily). Add haptic feedback with varying strengths for different actions (light for input clicks, heavy for tab changes). Choose consistent icon styles (e.g., Hero Icons thin version in budgeting app Luna) and use heavier/filled icons for selected states. Elevate design taste via constant exposure to good design on Twitter and the design resource Mobin. Emphasizes aggregating many small details to create a premium feel.

Description
In Episode 55, Damien and Jeremy unpack what the latest Suburb Data figures are showing across the Australian property market. They walk through the capital cities for both houses and units, covering changes in values, DSR scores, market cycle timing, stock on market, days on market, vacancy rates and rental growth.

The discussion highlights the strongest markets, the ones beginning to improve, and how the proposed federal tax changes may start flowing through the data over the coming months.

The episode also looks at what these trends could mean for investors and owner occupiers, including why yields, affordability and price point matter more than ever in the current environment. From the continued strength in Perth and Darwin to the emerging signs of improvement in parts of Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra, this is a practical snapshot of where the market stands right now and what may come next.

Video about resume tips for landing ML internships at companies like Google DeepMind, Amazon, and Nuro. Key advice: keep resume to one page (recruiters spend ~7 seconds), put skills at top instead of a summary, omit irrelevant info (hobbies, basic OS knowledge), order experience/projects by relevance, use bold keywords from job descriptions, quantify achievements (e.g., F1 score 39%, 95% success rate), link to LinkedIn/GitHub/personal website/blog, and 'sell yourself' without lying. Speaker claims interviews came from matching specific team needs: Google DeepMind for RL experience (reimplementing a reinforcement learning paper) in a multimodal learning research role, Amazon for graph neural network traffic flow modeling, and Nuro for combining graph networks with autonomous navigation. Main reason for Google DeepMind interview was using a non-conventional application route rather than standard applications.

LinkedIn's algorithm shifted from separate ranking models to a unified AI system evaluating profile...
LinkedIn's algorithm shifted from separate ranking models to a unified AI system evaluating profile, content, and engagement as a single signal via 'depth score' (reading time, saves, comment depth). Company pages reach only ~1.6% of followers; personal profiles drive 65% of feed. Audit criteria: profile headline (role, audience, outcome, searchable term), about section first 300 characters, feature slots (lead magnet, proof point, content sample), banner with transformation; content formats (PDFs, carousels, native video under 30s, long-form text 1,000–3,000 chars) boost depth score, avoid external links (60% reach drop), 80% real experience / 20% AI; engagement requires substantive comments (50x like weight), thread depth, niche alignment, authenticity (no pods). Audit workflow: screenshot criteria cards, gather page/profile inputs, use AI prompt to score and generate fixes, keyword strategy, and team briefing. HubSpot social team's about section scored 4/10.

0:00 – Intro / What we are covering

3:02 - Custom Illustrations (and animations)

#appdevelopment #dayinthelife #softwareengineer #startup #softwaredev #indieappdeveloper #dayinthelifecoding #codewithme #buildinpublic #vlog
Chris (productivity app developer) explains how to make apps feel premium through craft and taste, ...
Chris (productivity app developer) explains how to make apps feel premium through craft and taste, using his calorie-tracking app Amy (Apple Notes style) as a case study. Key topics: animation levels (no feedback, toast popups, refined custom animations like a purple-orange gradient for AI summarization; took 6 hours / 50+ prompts), illustration quality (hand-drawn Procreate illustrations by his wife Cecilia for Amy's onboarding vs generic AI images; advises 30+ prompts and mixing styles, using Midjourney sref inspiration, and animating images via Midjourney loop), working with human artists for uniqueness and storytelling (commissioned art for a few hundred dollars; hybrid workflow with AI derivatives used in unreleased app Lily), reverse-engineering ChatGPT's inline camera feature for Amy, and an invisible craft example: dictation in Amy adds 30 closest restaurants as context to correctly recognize hard-to-say restaurant names like Seul (Korean BBQ in Dallas) with this location feature opt-in. Tools/resources mentioned: Claude Code, Mobin for studying animations, Whisper Flow for voice-to-text dictation (works with Cursor/Windsurf, tags files), ChatGPT, Duolingo as a brand with unique illustration style. Core claims: AI's first output is the starting line, not finish line; unique/good requires heavy iteration; premium is felt more than seen; taste is the defining skill for the AI era. Takeaways: always ask 'can I make this better,' iterate hard, and focus on invisible craft that pleasantly surprises users.

This video explains how to break into AI engineering, distinguishing it from data science and ML en...
This video explains how to break into AI engineering, distinguishing it from data science and ML engineering: AI engineers build applications on pre-trained foundation models (e.g., GPT-5, Llama) using prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), fine-tuning, and AI agents, rather than training models from scratch. Target US salaries are $200k-$300k/year. Skills are broken into three tiers: foundational (production-level Python, Git, command line, APIs, basic ML concepts like supervised/unsupervised learning, overfitting), core AI engineering (AI APIs like OpenAI, prompt engineering, RAG with vector databases and embeddings, AI agents, deployment with Docker and AWS/GCP/Azure, monitoring/logging), and advanced (sophisticated RAG chunking/retrieval, LoRA fine-tuning, model selection trade-offs, prompt injection security, privacy/ethics). Learning paths include self-study (~$0-$1k, flexible but requires discipline), bootcamps/certificates ($5k-$20k, 3-12 months, e.g., SimplyLearn/Purdue applied generative AI program with LangChain, OpenAI, Hugging Face and seven industry projects), master's degrees ($10k-$100k+, criticized as outdated/theoretical but useful for resume screening), and PhDs (not recommended for AI engineering). Portfolio projects should avoid tutorials/Kaggle; instead build self-motivated end-to-end projects using real data (APIs, web scraping, niche datasets) with full pipelines: data collection, cleaning, model integration (API/fine-tuning/RAG), deployment, UI/monitoring, plus strong GitHub documentation and blogging. Job applications should lead with AI engineering keywords on resume/LinkedIn, and use personalized cold outreach (not asking for jobs directly) to recruiters/hiring managers or team members at target companies, referencing their technical blogs/papers to start dialogues. Realistic timeline from scratch part-time is 3-5 years: ~6 months for basics and first apps (add 6 months if no programming background), 6-12 more months for advanced concepts, 1-2 years to professional competence, 3-5 years to senior roles. The speaker is Marina, an applied ML worker at Amazon and career coach, who offered one-on-one mentoring.

Make your project accessible and impactful by creating a really nice GitHub repo with modular, welldocumented code. Write a compelling readme that explains why your project does what it does and why that matters. Include clear instructions for setting up and running your project. And ideally, make some kind of interactive UI. Then share your work as wide as you can. Write a blog post and share on LinkedIn Twitter Discord Reddit wherever. You could also create YouTube videos demonstrating your project, or even present at local meetups or conferences. The more you share your work, the more likely it is to be seen by potential employers or collaborators. All right, so now you have the skills and have demonstrated them through real end-to-end projects. It's time to start applying to jobs. When it comes to your resume and LinkedIn, structure your materials to lead with relevant content. Put your skill section first with all your AI engineering technologies highlighted right up top. Make your project section prominent and put your portfolio website link somewhere where it's clearly visible. For your LinkedIn headline, instead of saying something like student or aspiring AI engineer, use something like AI engineer building production LLM applications, rag, and finetuning. Write a summary with relevant keywords that positions you as already an AI engineer. All of this can help set you up for success in the traditional job application process. But unfortunately, if you lack industry experience, you may still get filtered out by automated resume screening systems. So, we need to get creative. At this point, I always recommend networking, but probably not how you think. It's not just about going to local meetups and hoping to meet someone, although that's great, too. We're actually going to proactively build up our network through non-pushy, cold outreach. And before you poo poo this, cold emails are how I got my first data science job with no experience. So, I know it can work. I suggest reaching out to people from two kinds of companies. First, companies that you see are hiring AI engineers, of course. And second, companies that you'd love to work for, whether or not they have open positions right now. If a company is actively hiring, you can reach out to the recruiter or the hiring manager. If they aren't, anyone on the team doing AI engineering is a good choice. Now, here's the thing. We are not going to just send a message on LinkedIn asking for a referral or saying that you'd love the job. We're actually not going to mention hiring at all. Instead, find something genuinely interesting that the company is doing. Read their technical blog, watch their YouTube, read their papers on archive. Then send them a message praising their work and asking some kind of detailed, informed question. Why did you take this approach versus another approach? What motivated this decision? Things like that. You're just trying to compliment them. Ask a smart question and open a dialogue. If they respond and you have some friendly, well-informed exchanges, then you can ask for feedback on your resume or a project or ask what skills they're looking for on their team or maybe even directly ask for a referral. I know this sounds scary, but I can say personally I'm never offended by a well-thoughtout personalized message. Though I do tend to ignore the pretty generic [music] ones. And honestly, the worst outcome is that nothing will happen. They'll just ignore you. But the potential upside is enormous. So, it's worth it. All right. So, as you can see, there's a lot involved with getting that first job. Many people ask me what's realistic in terms of a timeline. So, let's talk about that next. As you can see from this list of really technical concepts to learn and projects to build, you're not going to just go from an absolute beginner to a professional AI engineer in 3 months. Assuming you're working on this part-time and self-studying, here are some rough guidelines for how long each phase will take. Getting the basics down and building your first AI apps will probably take around 6 months. This assumes you're studying consistently and already have some programming background. If you're starting from absolute zero, add another 6 months. Becoming comfortable with more advanced concepts will probably be 6 to 12 more months. During this time, you should be building increasingly complex projects and deepening your understanding of the underlying technologies. Reaching professional level competence could be another 1 to two years. This is where you develop those specialized skills needed for roles at larger companies or more advanced AI applications. Becoming a senior or lead AI engineer at a top company where you'd really be earning $300,000 or more would be 3 to five additional years. Mastering the full spectrum of AI engineering skills and gaining the experience to lead complex projects takes significant time in the field. In total, expect a 3 to 5 year journey if you're starting from scratch and working part-time on your learning. Is that a long time? Yes, but it's also realistic. And remember, you can start building and potentially even working in the field much earlier than that. You don't have to wait until you've mastered everything to get started. I just say this because those who expect to become AI engineers in just a few months inevitably get discouraged when they discover the field's true complexity. But those who approach it with realistic expectations and focus on incremental progress often succeed and find themselves in high demand positions that didn't even exist a few years ago. If you want to dive deeper into any of these topics, I have detailed videos on building standout AI engineering projects, a complete AI engineering roadmap with a comprehensive skills checklist, and interview prep for AI and ML roles. Check those out. The links are in the description. And if you want personalized guidance, I offer one-on-one mentoring sessions. That link is in the description, too. Thank you so much for watching, and I'll see you next time.

Description
Everyone thinks the budget just blew up property investing forever, but here’s the twist: most of the dramatic headlines won’t touch your portfolio for years, if ever, with fears driving the market rather than reality.

On The Smart Property Investment Show, Liam Garman sits down with Arjun Paliwal, CEO of InvestorKit, to rip apart the panic and reveal what the federal budget really means for Australian property investors.

Paliwal drops a bombshell: despite the widespread freakout over negative gearing and capital gains tax, almost everyone is getting it wrong, and some investors are wildly exaggerating just how fast or how hard these changes will actually hit.

While seasoned investors with smart structures might dodge the worst of it, Paliwal warns that everyday investors and rentvesters could be the ones left exposed as the rules keep shifting beneath their feet.

The duo then dives into rising unemployment, looming interest rate uncertainty, and the economic curveballs that could reshape your borrowing power and investment moves for years to come.

Instead of panicking over fear-driven headlines, Paliwal says the real winners will be the investors who zoom out, build financial resilience, and figure out exactly how these changes apply to their own situation.

If you like this episode, show your support by rating us or leaving a review on Apple Podcasts and by following Smart Property Investment on social media: Facebook, X (formerly Twitter) and LinkedIn.

Video by Akash Gupta (Concepts of AI) explaining why ML internship resumes get rejected despite following generic advice. Key tips: treat GitHub as a second resume with clean READMEs, requirements.txt, and no exposed API keys/env files; explain projects like products with one-page PDF reports covering problem, tech, challenges, learnings; list applied skills (Python, NumPy, pandas, Flask, AWS EC2/S3) rather than broad subjects; keep formatting professional with no typos; customize resumes per role (data scientist vs ML engineer vs AI engineer); avoid overcrowding, focus on 6-8 solid skills; quantify impact with metrics like accuracy improvements, inference time reductions, dataset sizes; structure GitHub repos to look production-ready; prepare a master project summary doc for faster customization; keep resumes ATS-friendly and simple rather than creative poster-style designs.

Every YouTuber says the same thing. Keep your resume simple. Add projects. Use keywords and you follow all that. Upload it. But still there is silence. No calls, no emails and no a IML internships. But why? I used to wonder the same thing until I started talking to AI professionals working in the industry. My seniors from top companies. And after hundreds of resume rejections, finally I understood what they actually look for in a machine learning resume. Not the textbook advice, not those generic ATS hacks, but the real unspoken things that make recruiters stop scrolling and think, "Wait, this resume looks serious." Hello everyone, I Akash Gupta and this is Concepts of AI. And in this video, I'm going to give you the 10 tips that I personally used in my resume while applying for ML internships and they completely changed how recruiters saw me. Today I'm sharing them with you straight from experience not theory and stay till the end because the last tip will surprise you. So the first is your GitHub. Your GitHub is your second resume. So when you mention the projects in your resume, don't just mention them, prove them. Attach a GitHub link for every serious project you have done and please make it look professional. You should have in your GitHub repo proper readme files, requirements.txt file and clean code folders. I have seen students that they are very casual about these things but these things are important because professionals in industry use GitHub only. One more thing, never upload your env file or API keys on the GitHub repo publicly. It looks careless. A recruiter once told me that if a student uploads files publicly, I can't trust him with the production data. That is how serious it is. Second, explain your project like a product, not like a homework. Every project should have a one-page report or drive PDF link in your resume which should have what problem did you solve in this project, what text you used, what challenges did you face and what did you learn from those challenges. I still attach these minor reports in my resume links because while others show code I show clarity and that is what makes look like an AI engineer not a college student. Third is skill is not equal to subject. In your skill section in resume don't write things like machine learning or statistics under skills that is knowledge not a skill. Write how you apply that knowledge. You can write like Python having numpy pandas and psychic libraries deployment using flask and fast API cloud using AWS EC2 and S3. So when recruiters see tools not topics they know you have done real work not just taken a course. The fourth one, your resume is like your code. So here formatting is very important. So avoid the messy alignment, random fund sizes, grammatical mistakes. These are small things but they scream unprofessional and from my experience I'm telling you these things are very serious. One recruiter literally told me if a resume has typos don't we don't even check their projects. So always proofread with Grammarly, keep margins clean and don't experiment with font. Next is different roles having different stories. I have seen people applying for data scientist, ML engineer, AI engineer all with the same resume. That is the biggest mistake. Customize it. If it is for data scientist, show business impact and insights in your projects. If it is for ML engineer, you need to show pipelines, deployment and scalability. And if it is for AI engineer highlights like LLMs, use of APIs, embeddings, lenchen whatever is the latest tool in the market. So same person three stories that is how you fit every job perfectly. Next is you should have less cutter and more confidence in your resume. Overcrowded resumes are red flags. It feels like you are trying to prove everything at once. Keep six to eight solid skills but make your projects prove them. Depth beats density. Next is show numbers always. Recruiters love numbers. That is their language. Don't say that I built an ML model. Say improved accuracy from 72% to 86% using this ML algorithm or I reduce inference time by 30%. Or process 50,000 tweets for sentiment analysis. Numbers show impact and that is what gets you shortlisted. Eighth one, structure your GitHub like a pro. Your GitHub repo should look like this. That is given in the screen. You can see when a recruiter opens it, they should instantly feel that this person can handle production code. That impression alone can put you ahead of 90% of students. Again, I'm telling you in industry, they use GitHub. So, be very professional about it. The ninth one, keep a project summary doc with you before you apply. Keep one sheet with all your projects. Project text tech metrics, GitHub link, drive report. When you are customizing resumes, this becomes your shortcut to copy the right details fast. Most people panic before applying. This saves you hours. And the last one, resume is clarity, not creativity. I have reviewed tons of students resumes and half of them look like posters, gradient backgrounds, graphs, icons. Don't use them. Recruiters don't need art. They need information. So keep it simple, ATS friendly and clean because your resume is not supposed to impress. It is supposed to communicate. So these tips are the real reason I got shortlisted for my first ML internship. And trust me, they work. If you have been applying and not hearing back, try these. And of course, subscribe the concepts of AI if you want real industry backed guidance on a IML and career growth. No fluff, just real

Description
What are the secrets to writing a resume that will get you noticed by top tech companies? I'll cover everything from choosing the right keywords to optimizing your experience section.
While coding projects are important for learning, your experience is the most valuable asset in getting a job. Focus on highlighting your achievements and the skills you used to accomplish them. 
To optimize your resume for the ATS, reference our Do’s and Don’ts list. 
Avoid cramming in every skill; only include those that directly relate to the target role. You can increase your chances of landing an interview by identifying the target role and tailoring your resume accordingly. A well-crafted resume not only showcases your qualifications but also demonstrates your understanding of the company's needs. 
I hope this video helps you land your dream job!

Recruiter explains resume screening methodology: 20-second scan, hiring managers hunt for qualifica...
Recruiter explains resume screening methodology: 20-second scan, hiring managers hunt for qualifications (what/how/why/result) not skill-section keywords. Uses 'hamburger vs hot dog' metaphor for relevance. Reviews AI engineer (needs AI/LLM/NLP/Python/Agents/LangChain/RAG/PyTorch), full-stack engineer (needs TS/JS/React/Node/SQL/cloud), Java engineer (needs Java/Spring/Maven/SQL/REST/microservices/CI-CD/cloud), data engineer (needs Python/ETL/SQL/cloud/Spark/Kafka), and project manager (needs PMP/CSM/numbers/agile/Jira). Describes ideal application-to-interview ratio (7:1), warns about 150+ applications. Emphasizes following specific resume format (linked in description), stating location, and avoiding implied skills. Advises international applicants (30-100:1) and fully remote roles (1:40).

Machine learning operations (MLOps) is an important process to make sure Machine Learning applications remain operational, but before you apply the same process to your large language models (LLM), Martin explains why and how LLMs need to be treated differently and the process known as LLMOps

Get started for free on IBM Cloud → https://ibm.biz/sign-up-now
Subscribe to see more videos like this in the future → http://ibm.biz/subscribe-now
This video explains LLMOps (Large Language Model Operations) as the operational management of LLMs ...
This video explains LLMOps (Large Language Model Operations) as the operational management of LLMs in production, distinct from broader MLOps. It covers the LLMOps lifecycle components: exploratory data analysis (EDA), data prep, prompt engineering, fine-tuning foundation models, model review/governance, inference/serving, and monitoring (including human feedback and detecting drift/attacks). Key differences from traditional ML include reliance on transfer learning/fine-tuning instead of training from scratch, hyperparameter tuning for cost/compute reduction, and specialized evaluation metrics like BLEU and ROUGE rather than accuracy/AUC/F1. The video highlights collaboration across data scientists, DevOps, and IT, and lists benefits: improved efficiency, reduced risk via security/privacy, and easier scalability.

You've applied to hundreds of jobs. Nothing. Not even a rejection email.
It's not you. It's the mistakes no one ever told you about.

As an ex-Google recruiter who's reviewed thousands of resumes and sat in countless hiring meetings, I'm exposing the 6 hidden reasons your resume gets rejected before anyone even reads it.

▶ You'll discover:

Why the "perfect" candidate rarely gets hired (and who does instead)
The deadly resume gaps that make recruiters create their own story about you
How using the wrong verbs instantly makes you look junior
Why your 15 years of experience might be working against you
The 3-part formula that makes any resume feel complete

Stop wondering if you're the problem. Start understanding what hiring managers actually want: someone who looks safe, sounds senior, and signals they can solve today's problems.

These aren't tips. These are the unspoken rules that get you interviews.

Resume mistakes: hiring managers want a 'safe pair of hands'—avoid vagueness, show clear results. E...
Resume mistakes: hiring managers want a 'safe pair of hands'—avoid vagueness, show clear results. Explain gaps or short stints upfront to reduce risk. Translate transferable skills into the target role's language. Use ownership verbs (led, drove) to signal seniority. Focus on last 5-7 years; cut older roles. Balance technical credibility, business impact, and leadership. Example: from 'handled operational duties' to 'cut costs by 15% by streamlining vendor contracts'.

You've applied to hundreds of jobs. You tweak your resume, rewrite the bullet points, fix the format, but still nothing. And at some point, you stop thinking about the resume, and you start wondering if you're the problem. The real reason you're getting ghosted is because of mistakes almost everybody makes. And no one tells you about it. So, in this video, I'll show you secrets about what's really getting your resume rejected before it even gets read. And after reading thousands of resumes in my career and sitting in hiring meetings, I can tell you this is what will actually get you interviews. Secret number one, managers hire safe pairs of hands. You probably assume hiring managers want the smartest, most qualified candidate with the most accomplished resume, but they don't. They just want someone who feels safe, someone who can step in and solve problems without creating more. Because most managers are already drowning in work. They're behind on deadlines, stressed about their own deliverables, and now on top of that, they have to hire, too. They're looking for the person who they know won't make things worse, who will make their job easier. That means your resume has one job. Make yourself look like a safe pair of hands. But most résumés do the opposite. They're vague or they're just filled with buzzwords or keywords. and they read like a list of random tasks with no outcomes. And when a resume feels even a little risky, it gets rejected. Not because you aren't qualified, but because of how you presented yourself. So, here's the fix. Every bullet on your resume should make you look like someone who's already done the job. You want to show recent, relevant, clear results. Things that communicate, "I've done this before and I can do it again." Here are the examples of bullet points. Here's a bad one. handled various operational duties over five years. What does that even mean? That's vague. That's risky. Here's a better bullet point. Cut operating costs by 15% Q2 2024 by streamlining vendor contracts, then providing some details about the vendor or the contracts. Now, I know what you did, the impact you had, and that you can probably do it for me. If your resume makes you look like a safe pair of hands, you're already ahead of most candidates. But even if you're safe, the language you're using is making you look junior. And that's the next mistake. Secret number two, explain risk on the page, not in the interview. Let me tell you what recruiters never do. They never stop to investigate a vague resume. Before you complain, "Well, recruiters are lazy." They're not. Imagine you have to get through 200 rs in a day and on top of that all the calls and all the meetings you have. They're not lazy, they're short on time. So, if something in your resume is vague or raises questions like a gap, a pivot, a short stint, or a weird transition and you don't explain it, we're going to make up our own story. Most people think that being vague makes them look safer. Like, if I don't mention it, they won't notice. But in recruiting, silence equals risk. Because when a resume is unclear, it's going to slow me down. And when I'm screening this many, I don't have time for confusion. So, here's the shift. Your resume should briefly explain the risky stuff upfront. If you took time off to care for a parent, say so in the summary. If you left a job after 3 months, give a oneline reason in your work experience. You don't need to overshare. You just need to make recruiters understand what happened. Here's a bad example. Operations Manager, March 2022 to May 2022. No context, no explanation. Here's a better bullet point. Operations Manager, March 2022 to May 2022. Position impacted by departmental reorganization seeking a role with long-term growth. Now I understand. Now you feel safe. And if you have a gap, like a career break, January 2023 to June 2023, family caregiving responsibilities now available full-time, that's simple, clear, with no mystery. If you don't explain your story, someone else will and they'll get it wrong. But even when your story is clear, the language you use to tell it still matters. That's what we'll get into next. Secret number three, transferable skills are useless without translation. You know you can do the job. You've got the skills, the experience, the results. But if you're applying outside of your current industry or you're shifting roles, here's the problem. Recruiters don't read your resume to decode your potential. They read it to look for signals that they already recognize. So even if your experience technically fits and you're not using the right language, you won't get considered. So here's the fix. Every bullet needs to translate your past experience into their business priorities. That means scanning the job description and mirroring their verbiage so you sound like someone who's already in their world and in that role. So, here's some examples. Here's a bad one. Led weekly ops syncs to resolve escalations between regional managers. This sounds really internal. It's very jargony and has no context. Here's a better one. Resolve high priority operational issues across 12 markets, reducing delay time by 30% and improving team delivery scores by 12%. Now you sound like someone who drives outcomes, not someone stuck in internal meetings. If the right person reads the wrong words, it doesn't matter how good you are. And even if you do use the right language, your resume might still look interchangeable. That's the next mistake. If you're enjoying this video, go ahead and give it a like. And if you want to learn more recruiter secrets, go ahead and click subscribe. Secret number four, the words you use define how senior you look. If your bullets start with help, supported, or worked on, you're signaling that you weren't leading. Even if you were qualified, even if you are running the show, that language makes you sound like a passenger. So, here's the fix. Here are some examples. Here's a bad one. Worked on a migration project for internal tools. Tools for what? What do those tools even do? I have no context. Secret number six, résumés need more than one kind of strength. You might have the skills, the results, the leadership, but if your resume only shows one type of strength, you don't look complete. And that's the trap because you're missing something because you're only showing one side of yourself. If your resume leans too technical, you look like a builder without direction. Too strategic and you sound like fluff. We wonder if you can actually roll up your sleeves and get the job done. Video provides a software engineering resume checklist covering formatting, ATS optimization, section-by-section guidance (personal info, summary, skills, work experience/projects, education). Key claims: avoid fancy templates (ATS cannot parse), keep to one page, use standard fonts (Arial, Calibri), tailor summary per job using keywords from job description, list only relevant specialized skills (not a generalist list), include metrics in bullet points (even if BS), exclude generic school projects. Recommends tools like hired.dev, jobright, massive.com, and Fang Tech leads for ATS tips. Emphasizes small details (grammar, location, consistent spacing) as red flags for recruiters. Target audience: software engineers facing a tough job market.

Description
Most investors are still reacting to the headlines. But buried in the fine print? The biggest tax overhaul in 26 years, with holding behaviour and investment structures already starting to reshape how property decisions are made.

Property accountant Jeremy Iannuzzelli joins Kev Tran on the KTG Property Podcast to break down what the federal budget actually means for Australian investors and why the window to act strategically may be closing fast.

Negative gearing, capital gains tax (CGT), trusts, and self-managed super funds (SMSFs) – every major lever is being adjusted at once, and investors who fail to adapt risk being left behind while others quietly reposition.

The duo explains that changes to negative gearing could reshape investor behaviour by encouraging longer hold periods and tightening supply in key markets, while the return to indexation-style CGT calculations could materially alter long-term strategy around exits and portfolio restructuring.

Attention then turns to trusts and SMSFs, with the pair highlighting a noticeable shift toward superannuation structures as investors search for more tax-efficient ways to continue building property portfolios.

Despite the uncertainty, Iannuzzelli argues the investors who stay strategic and deliberate, rather than reactive, will be the ones best positioned to navigate and potentially benefit from the next phase of the market.

Podcast interview with property accountant/investor Jeremy Izzaly analyzing the 2024 Australian fed...
Podcast interview with property accountant/investor Jeremy Izzaly analyzing the 2024 Australian federal budget's property tax changes. Covers: (1) negative gearing grandfathered for pre-budget properties, only available for new builds from 1 July 2027; (2) reintroduction of capital gains tax indexation for assets held after 1 July 2027, with a 50% CGT discount for pre-27 gains; (3) 30% flat tax on trust distributions and bucket company traps; (4) minimum 30% tax on CGT for low-income earners. Key claims: migration (2.4M arrivals 2026-30) underpins demand; grandfathered assets won't be sold, reducing supply; consumer sentiment low (high 70s-low 80s) signals buying opportunity; SMSFs remain attractive due to 10% effective CGT rate; commercial property unaffected by changes. Dates: budget night 12 May 2024, 1 July 2027, Senate inquiry 22 June 2024.

Description
What if your LinkedIn profile could bring job offers to you—without sending a single application? In this step-by-step LinkedIn tutorial, you'll learn how to optimize every part of your profile to attract recruiters, hiring managers, and potential clients. From taking the perfect profile picture to writing a standout headline and summary, you'll discover actionable tips that make your profile work 24/7 to promote you.

I’ll also show how you can enhance your photos using AI tools like ChatGPT and give real examples from my role at the Kevin Cookie Company. Plus, you'll learn how to post updates to stay top-of-mind in your network and unlock hidden features like custom URLs and the “Open to Work” option.

Whether you're job hunting, building your personal brand, or growing your business, this LinkedIn profile makeover will set you apart in 2025 and beyond.

Video showcases 9 free UI component libraries and templates for web/mobile apps. Key items: Liquid ...
Video showcases 9 free UI component libraries and templates for web/mobile apps. Key items: Liquid Metal (animated liquid metal border component); Access (free B2B SaaS template with light/dark mode) and Noha (consumer app template with forest green/sunny orange themes) from style.dev; SkipperUI (free/paid components including image hover cards, Star Wars-style end credits animation, stacked cards, card swipes, and an expanding video player); Alimom components (shaders, bento grids, iPhone/iPad device mockups, logo reels, typewriter effect, Apple Intelligence-style glow, gauge components); Watermelon UI (springy Apple-like animations, onboarding-style components, card swiper); Cult UI (colorful hero sections, animated family button, lightboard, dot matrix loaders); componentry.fun (tactile keyboard with keypress sounds, flight status tracker, GitHub tracker, matrix-style effects). Also mentions balloonjs for balloon pop-up animations. Claims: all featured components/templates are free, installation can be delegated to AI agents, and users can ask AI to extract a design system from a single component to make the rest of the site match. Sponsor segment covers CodeRabbit, an AI code review agent used at NVIDIA (with a Jensen Huang quote), including a new CLI workflow that reviews code before creating a PR.

Agentic engineering workflow by Kun (ex-Meta/Microsoft/Atlassian L8 principal engineer). Core setup...
Agentic engineering workflow by Kun (ex-Meta/Microsoft/Atlassian L8 principal engineer). Core setup: terminal-centric workflow using Western, Tmux, NeoVim for keyboard-only flow. Four agent harnesses: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Pi coding agent, Open Code. Onboarding via global/project-level memory files and progressive-disclosure skills. Voice input via Super Whisperer. Lavish tool for rich planning with HTML artifacts. No Mistakes pipeline for automated PR creation, adversarial review, end-to-end testing, and babysitting. Good Night Have Fun for long-running autonomous tasks (e.g., overnight). Treehouse for isolated git work trees enabling parallel agents. First Mate orchestrates multiple parallel tasks, context-switches between projects, manages work trees and pipelines. Goal: shift from individual contributor to captain, scaling to 40-50 PRs/day by focusing on strategy while agents execute.

The video presents a workflow for achieving consistent UI design when building apps with AI. It con...
The video presents a workflow for achieving consistent UI design when building apps with AI. It contrasts a messy app (Pluto) due to missing design system with a consistent workflow. Core concepts: design systems (single source of truth: components, guidelines, brand identity) and design tokens (variables like spacing-medium, color-brand-primary) enabling theming (e.g., dark mode) and centralized maintenance. Workflow steps: (1) collect inspiration from Twitter bookmarks, Gather OS, Mobin, or sites like family.co; (2) create a design system in Claw Design (AI tool) by uploading a screenshot or using Vercel's design.md as a base, prompting it to generate components and display tokens; (3) tweak the design system via markup and chat edits until satisfied; (4) export/share to Claude Code (MCP import), which then builds pages (landing, sign-up/sign-in, dashboard) consistently from the design system; (5) optionally add UI libraries like BUI for micro-animations while still using the design system tokens. Claims: AI-generated design without a design system feels 'fugly' and inconsistent; fixing one token updates everywhere. Mentioned tools: Claw Design, Claude Code, SvelteKit, Zen browser, Gather OS, Mobin, BUI, Vercel design.md. Mentions sponsors (Scribba) and personal tangents.

Hosts Damian and Jeremy discuss capital city metrics: DSR 3, typical value, stock on market, days on market, vacancy rates, rental growth. 2gXf7fRvuaXAThe strategy to win after this budgetSmart Property Investment0.4854-0.0292yesyesPodcast interview with property accountant/investor Jeremy Izzaly analyzing the 2024 Australian federal budget's property tax changes. Covers: (1) negative gearing grandfathered for pre-budget properties, only available for new builds from 1 July 2027; (2) reintroduction of capital gains tax indexation for assets held after 1 July 2027, with a 50% CGT discount for pre-27 gains; (3) 30% flat tax on trust distributions and bucket company traps; (4) minimum 30% tax on CGT for low-income earners. Key claims: migration (2.4M arrivals 2026-30) underpins demand; grandfathered assets won't be sold, reducing supply; consumer sentiment low (high 70s-low 80s) signals buying opportunity; SMSFs remain attractive due to 10% effective CGT rate; commercial property unaffected by changes. Dates: budget night 12 May 2024, 1 July 2027, Senate inquiry 22 June 2024.
3cvPEiPt7HXoLarge Language Model Operations (LLMOps) ExplainedIBM Technology0.1624-0.6752nonoThis video explains LLMOps (Large Language Model Operations) as the operational management of LLMs in production, distinct from broader MLOps. It covers the LLMOps lifecycle components: exploratory data analysis (EDA), data prep, prompt engineering, fine-tuning foundation models, model review/governance, inference/serving, and monitoring (including human feedback and detecting drift/attacks). Key differences from traditional ML include reliance on transfer learning/fine-tuning instead of training from scratch, hyperparameter tuning for cost/compute reduction, and specialized evaluation metrics like BLEU and ROUGE rather than accuracy/AUC/F1. The video highlights collaboration across data scientists, DevOps, and IT, and lists benefits: improved efficiency, reduced risk via security/privacy, and easier scalability.
41jvxxa7tdjwExploring MLOps and LLMOps: Architectures and Best PracticesDatabricks0.1344-0.7312nonoDatabricks MLOps and LMOps architecture best practices. MLOps combines data ops, DevOps, and model ops; key practices include role separation (business stakeholder, data engineer, data scientist, ML engineer, data governance officer), environment isolation across dev/staging/prod, promoting code (not just models) for reproducibility and production data lockdown, Unity Catalog for centralized governance/lineage of tables, features, models, and inference tables, plus model serving (real-time APIs, A/B testing, canary deployments, request/response logging) and monitoring for drift. Databricks MLOps Stacks provide a customizable CI/CD framework integrating GitHub/Azure DevOps. For LMOps: RAG architectures using vector search, feature serving, foundation model APIs, CPU model serving for chains, MLflow tracing and evaluation (LLM-as-a-judge metrics, answer relevance, human feedback logging), config-based LangChain chains, auto-synced vector indexes, and inference/feedback tables for monitoring and fine-tuning. Pre-training/fine-tuning stacks include Mosaic AI model training, Composer, streaming datasets, LLM Foundry, evaluation gauntlet, and DBRX, with Spark/Delta/Unity Catalog remaining core. AI security guidance referenced via Databricks whitepaper.

10UxVM1xDBdt4How to Get Your First AI Engineering Job (skills, projects, resumes, and more)Marina Wyss - AI & Machine Learning0.0593-0.8813nonoThis video explains how to break into AI engineering, distinguishing it from data science and ML engineering: AI engineers build applications on pre-trained foundation models (e.g., GPT-5, Llama) using prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), fine-tuning, and AI agents, rather than training models from scratch. Target US salaries are $200k-$300k/year. Skills are broken into three tiers: foundational (production-level Python, Git, command line, APIs, basic ML concepts like supervised/unsupervised learning, overfitting), core AI engineering (AI APIs like OpenAI, prompt engineering, RAG with vector databases and embeddings, AI agents, deployment with Docker and AWS/GCP/Azure, monitoring/logging), and advanced (sophisticated RAG chunking/retrieval, LoRA fine-tuning, model selection trade-offs, prompt injection security, privacy/ethics). Learning paths include self-study (~$0-$1k, flexible but requires discipline), bootcamps/certificates ($5k-$20k, 3-12 months, e.g., SimplyLearn/Purdue applied generative AI program with LangChain, OpenAI, Hugging Face and seven industry projects), master's degrees ($10k-$100k+, criticized as outdated/theoretical but useful for resume screening), and PhDs (not recommended for AI engineering). Portfolio projects should avoid tutorials/Kaggle; instead build self-motivated end-to-end projects using real data (APIs, web scraping, niche datasets) with full pipelines: data collection, cleaning, model integration (API/fine-tuning/RAG), deployment, UI/monitoring, plus strong GitHub documentation and blogging. Job applications should lead with AI engineering keywords on resume/LinkedIn, and use personalized cold outreach (not asking for jobs directly) to recruiters/hiring managers or team members at target companies, referencing their technical blogs/papers to start dialogues. Realistic timeline from scratch part-time is 3-5 years: ~6 months for basics and first apps (add 6 months if no programming background), 6-12 more months for advanced concepts, 1-2 years to professional competence, 3-5 years to senior roles. The speaker is Marina, an applied ML worker at Amazon and career coach, who offered one-on-one mentoring.

Takeaways: always ask 'can I make this better,' iterate hard, and focus on invisible craft that pleasantly surprises users.
